analysis.one_liner: Lets states cap interest rates on loans made by banks and credit unions chartered in that state.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 31-18 in September 2026; it has not yet received a vote by the full House.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, a bank or credit union can charge the interest rate of the state where it is chartered, no matter how strict the borrower's own state's rate caps are. This bill would let a state shut off that privilege — but only for banks and credit unions chartered in that state. If a state passed a law, or its voters approved one, saying it does not want rate exportation for its home-state lenders, those lenders could no longer charge another state's (usually higher) rates on loans made in that state. It also repeals a 1980 federal law that let states opt out only for national banks, a tool that has largely gone unused.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in any state whose voters or legislature opt out would gain protection from high interest rates on loans from that state's own banks and credit unions. States would regain a power they lost decades ago to cap rates charged by lenders they charter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states that opt out

how_it_helps.text: Today, a state-chartered bank headquartered in another state can 'export' its home state's interest rate into your state, even if your state caps rates. This bill closes that path for your own state's chartered lenders.
A state could act either by passing a law or by certifying a vote of its own people, so borrowers could pressure state legislatures — or vote directly — to restore rate caps on home-state lenders.
The change would apply to state banks, credit unions, and would also apply to state laws already adopted before enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions chartered in an opting-out state would lose the ability to charge out-of-state interest rates on loans made there, which could mean lower revenue and, lenders argue, less credit available to risky borrowers.

drawbacks.text: Banks in an opt-out state could respond by raising rates on all their loans or tightening credit, since they would lose the ability to charge one uniform national rate; borrowers with poor credit could find fewer lenders willing to serve them.

The bill repeals the 1980 federal law outright and applies retroactively to state laws and voter certifications adopted before enactment, which could unsettle existing loan agreements and invite litigation over which loans are covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but conditional: it only helps borrowers in states willing to take the politically and legally demanding step of overriding their own banks' rate-export advantage. The costs are that lenders in opt-out states may reduce lending to riskier borrowers, and the rollback of the 1980 law could invite litigation and cross-state confusion during a transition. The bill does not itself cap any rate; it merely restores states' authority to do so, which makes its real-world effect depend entirely on future state action.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee voted 31-18 to advance the bill in September 2026, but the full House has not voted on it and the session is still running.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2026, and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
On September 16, 2026, the committee held a markup and voted 31-18 to order the bill reported to the full House with amendments.
As of the available record, no further action has been taken and the full House has not considered the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost; the bill cleared committee but faces an uncertain path to a House floor vote, and lenders keep the status quo until then.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup and voted 31-18 to order the bill reported to the House with amendments.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has both Republican and Democratic cosponsors (3 Republicans and 4 Democrats), and the committee vote of 31-18 did not split cleanly along party lines in the available record.

industries.industry: State-chartered banks and credit unions (in states that opt out)
industries.note: In states that opt out, these lenders could no longer charge out-of-state rates on home-state loans, capping a key revenue source. Nationwide, the bill only threatens this revenue where states choose to act.

The bill does not touch the federal preemption that lets national banks export rates, so they could keep charging out-of-state rates in opt-out states — potentially gaining a competitive edge over in-state banks that are capped.

analysis.trajectory: The bill cleared committee with a comfortable 31-18 vote, which is real progress, but most bills that pass committee never reach the House floor; its fate now depends on leadership scheduling it for a vote.
